_comment: Conformance cases for judge, the fallbacks and the walk. Taken from datrail/gateway's gateway-core/tests/vectors/v2/decide.json (its whole-bundle cases) and fallback.json, at 6758b77; bundles are filled in to the 2.0 shape Rail Center publishes, both fallbacks `pass` unless a case is about one, and claims to the typed claims. fallback.json's `<slug>.<tool>` keys are rewritten to `<slug>#/mcp#tools/call#<tool>`, and its cases with no chain are given one inert alert. An `endpoint` is `keyless`, `unrecognised` or {"resolved": key}, the key without its slug. `expect.fallbacks` lists the fallbacks that deny, in the order asked, and `expect.chain` the walk's verdict, null where a fallback denies at enforce; a refusal names the policy it was reached at. Removed: 5 with an action other than block or alert, which the contract denies on and this reader refuses with the bundle (Rail Center only publishes the two); 2 with an `enabled` missing or not a boolean, which the contract reads as enabled and this reader refuses with the bundle (Rail Center always sends a boolean); 2 with mode none, where the caller never calls the judge. Cases marked `added` are this reader's own: the ticket fallback, which the frozen vectors predate, and narrowing order. A case marked `retargeted` says how it was moved onto a claim the typed claims hold.

cases.name: an endpoint with no binding entry is subject to every policy
cases.note: Read the other way round it is a total loss of enforcement, which is why the contract states it twice.

cases.name: a binding narrows to the policies it names
cases.note: The low-score rule matches and is not in this endpoint's chain.

cases.name: a binding in mode open narrows to nothing and the walk allows
cases.note: **Do not fall back to the whole chain when narrowing empties it.** Rail Center has a fallback of exactly that shape and it belongs to the publishing side alone: it drops a binding whose policies are all absent or disabled before the bundle is written. Copying it here makes the two sides disagree — deny there, allow here.

cases.name: a binding naming only a disabled policy narrows to nothing too
cases.note: The same empty narrowing by the other route, and the one a publishing-side fallback would turn into a denial by the whole chain.

cases.name: a bound id spelled non-canonically still narrows
cases.note: Both sides of the membership test are canonicalised, so a non-canonically spelled id matches its policy rather than nothing.

cases.name: the first matching denying policy wins and stops the walk
cases.note: A lower priority number is genuinely higher precedence rather than merely earlier in a list that keeps being read.

cases.name: priority 9 precedes priority 10
cases.note: Numerically, not as text: a default string comparator gets this backwards.

cases.name: equal priorities are separated by the canonical id
cases.note: An implementation reading two equal priorities must not be free to choose, or the two sides disagree exactly where the policies conflict.

cases.name: a non-canonically spelled id is reported canonically
cases.note: A decision reporting the bundle's own spelling names the same policy two ways across a decision and its denial report.

cases.name: the denial names the policy that actually matched
cases.note: An implementation reporting the first rule in its chain produces a record that is wrong and that nothing downstream will contradict.

cases.name: alerts that accumulated before a denial travel with it
cases.note: An alert that matched on a request a later denial stopped is still something an operator asked to be told about.

cases.name: alerts accumulate in evaluation order, not in the order the bundle listed them
cases.note: Listed at priorities [2, 3, 1] precisely so a reader that accumulates in bundle order fails it.

cases.name: an alert never denies
a policy that matches nothing denies nothing
an empty chain allows
a chain of only disabled policies allows
cases.note: A disabled policy is skipped, not evaluated and discarded.

cases.name: a disabled policy's condition is never read
cases.note: The remedy for a rule nobody can read is to switch it off, and that only works if disabling is decided before interpreting.

cases.name: a rule the walk never reaches changes nothing
cases.note: **The refusal is lazy.** The walk stops at the first match, so a rule at priority 9 is never reached once priority 1 has denied, and that request has a clean answer. Refusing the whole bundle up front turns one bad condition into a total outage and answers differently here.

cases.name: a rule the walk does reach refuses the request, alerts and all
cases.note: What separates 'refuse the request' from 'refuse but keep the alerts' and from 'skip the rule and keep walking'. Alerts already accumulated are discarded with the decision: they were the first half of a verdict that was never reached.

cases.name: a rule behind an unreadable one is never consulted
cases.note: The refusal comes first in the chain, so the walk ends there whatever the later rule would have answered.

cases.name: the seeded chain denies a request carrying no ticket
the seeded chain denies a low-scoring agent by the rule for it
a chain on the nested claims denies by level and alerts on drift, in evaluation order

policies.name: Deny an agent with no baseline

cases.name: the seeded chain allows a scored agent presenting a valid ticket
an unscored agent is denied by a rule about an absent score
cases.note: A null score is an absent one. A reader that lets a null read as present stops this rule firing on exactly the agents it exists for — and `lt 40` would not catch them either, since an ordered operator does not hold against an absence.

cases.name: an unscored agent is not caught by the low-score rule
cases.note: The other half of the pair above, and why the seeded chain needs both rules rather than one.

cases.name: enforce and block refuse an endpoint with no binding entry
cases.note: The rule the whole file is about. No entry, so the fallback answers and the chain is never reached.

cases.name: enforce and block refuse it however many other endpoints are bound
cases.note: A bundle with bindings is not a bundle where every endpoint is bound. Reading a non-empty `bindings` as 'this bundle narrows, so walk it' refuses nothing here.

cases.name: enforce and block do not refuse a gated endpoint
cases.note: An entry exists, so the fallback has nothing to say and the binding narrows as it always does.

cases.name: enforce and block do not refuse an open endpoint
cases.note: `open` is an entry. An endpoint an operator deliberately exempted is not one nobody has reviewed, and the most restrictive posture must not convert the one into the other.

cases.name: enforce and pass hand an unbound endpoint to the chain
cases.note: Not refused for being unbound — which is not the same as unjudged. The whole chain still judges it, and may still deny.

cases.name: enforce and pass change nothing for a bound endpoint
observe never consults a block fallback
cases.note: The half an implementation gets wrong. `observe` is what an operator uses to be sure nothing is blocked; a fallback consulted here blocks.

cases.name: observe never consults a pass fallback either
a message naming no tool by design is not an unbound endpoint
cases.note: There is no endpoint, so a fallback about endpoints has nothing to refuse. Refusing here would let the strictest posture close the messages a session opens with.

cases.name: a call whose tool name resolved to no key is refused under block
cases.note: It named an endpoint; the reader declined to compose a key for it. No binding can match a key that was never composed, and the input a reader understands least is not the one to give the benefit of the doubt.

cases.name: a call whose tool name resolved to no key is judged under pass
cases.note: The other half: `pass` hands it to the whole chain, which is where the endpoint-derived rules catch it.

cases.name: a message naming no tool by design is judged under pass too
enforce and pass: an unbound endpoint the chain denies is denied by the chain
cases.note: The half that stops `pass` being read as `unjudged`. The fallback does not refuse the call and the chain then does, so a reader that forwarded an unbound endpoint without walking it would answer `refused: false` correctly here and still admit the request the chain denies.

cases.name: enforce and pass: an unbound endpoint no policy matches is allowed
cases.note: The other half, and why the one above is not simply `block` by another name. Same bundle, same endpoint, same absence of a binding — only the ticket differs, so the verdict is the chain's and not the fallback's.

cases.name: enforce and block refuse before a chain that would have allowed
cases.note: The same request the case above allows. `block` refuses it without consulting the chain, which is what makes 'the chain is not consulted' observable: consult it and this call is allowed.

cases.name: narrowing keeps the chain order, not the order the binding lists ids in
enforce and a block ticket fallback deny a call with no usable ticket, without the chain
observe and a block ticket fallback still walk the chain, with every ticket path absent
a pass ticket fallback walks the chain with every ticket path absent
at observe, both fallbacks that would deny are reported, the ticket fallback first
at enforce, the ticket fallback answers before the binding fallback
a usable ticket never meets the ticket fallback
